addressed_problems.content: The paper's rewinding-IMP procedure requires training the dense network one or more times to locate a pruning mask and the rewinding iteration k. This repeated training is computationally expensive, limiting practical applicability. The unresolved scientific gap is whether efficient methods can be developed that identify equally-capable subnetworks at an early iteration without full training, perhaps using one-shot sensitivity criteria or other lightweight signals. Resolving this would enable the practical benefits of early pruning without the overhead of multiple training runs.

For deeper networks (e.g., ResNet-50, VGG-19), iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding to early training iterations yields winning tickets, but resetting to initialization (iteration 0) does not. It remains an open question whether equally-capable subnetworks truly exist at initialization and are merely undetected by IMP, or whether their absence is intrinsic to the optimization landscape. Determining which case holds requires either improved search methods that can detect such subnetworks if they exist, or theoretical characterization establishing why trainability at initialization is inherently limited for certain architectures and sparsity levels.

All experiments in this work are limited to image classification benchmarks (CIFAR-10 and ImageNet). It is an open question whether the phenomena of rewinding-era subnetworks that match full-network accuracy and the associated stability metrics generalize to other domains such as natural language processing, reinforcement learning, or generative models. The optimization dynamics and architectural designs in these domains differ substantially, so confirming the existence and properties of early-training subnetworks there is necessary to assess the universality of the lottery ticket hypothesis with rewinding.

The core pruning technique used is unstructured magnitude pruning, which does not directly yield execution speedups on commodity hardware or with standard deep learning libraries because it requires sparse matrix operations that are not efficiently supported. The unresolved issue is how to extend these findings to structured pruning techniques (e.g., channel pruning, filter pruning) or to develop hardware-aware sparse training methods that exploit the opportunity to prune early in training. Doing so would translate the demonstrated accuracy-sparsity tradeoffs into actual computational savings during training and inference.

While the paper demonstrates a strong correlation between subnetwork stability (both to pruning and to data order) and final accuracy, a theoretical explanation for why a small amount of early training produces such a large improvement in subnetwork trainability is not established. In particular, it remains an open question whether subnetworks that are more stable to pruning truly lie in the same basin of attraction as the dense model, and how gradient noise and optimization dynamics during the earliest iterations shape this effect. A mechanistic theory is needed to understand the role of the rewinding iteration in enabling trainable sparse subnetworks.

The paper manually selects the rewinding iteration k based on empirical observation (e.g., epoch 6 for ResNet-50 on ImageNet). The development of principled criteria to automatically determine the optimal rewind iteration, and whether such criteria generalize across different random seeds, architectures, datasets, and sparsity levels, is left unresolved. Addressing this would remove the need for manual tuning and enable the practical deployment of rewinding-based pruning without extensive hyperparameter search.

For neural-network pruning, the prior scientific baseline is that pruning is an effective post-training compression tool but that pruning before or at initialization to produce sparse networks that can be trained from scratch is unresolved for realistic, deep architectures. Existing approaches fall into two broad camps: (1) post-training pruning and retraining, which demonstrates that many parameters are unnecessary for inference but does not reduce the cost of the original training process; and (2) pruning-at-or-before-initialization methods (including iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) with reset-to-init, single-shot sensitivity methods like SNIP, and reinitialize-and-train results) that attempt to identify small trainable subnetworks up-front. These pruning-at-or-before-initialization approaches have demonstrated success only on small or lightly pruned settings and rely on different, sometimes brittle, remedies (e.g., bespoke learning-rate schedules, warmup, or reinitialization heuristics). Specifically, iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) when used with resetting-to-iteration-0 (the procedure used to find "winning tickets") fails to produce subnetworks that train to the same accuracy for many deeper networks and larger tasks (e.g., ResNet-18 / VGG-19 on CIFAR-10 under standard schedules; ImageNet-scale networks), and alternative methods either do not scale to such depths/tasks or require maintaining much of the dense network for most of training. As a consequence, the field lacks (a) a principled, empirically validated characterization of when and why small subnetworks exist early in the training trajectory for deep, large-scale networks, and (b) practical pruning procedures that can locate such subnetworks early enough in training to reduce the computational cost of training large models. This gap prevents confident claims about pruning-before-training for deep architectures and leaves open whether the failures reflect the nonexistence of trainable subnetworks at initialization or only failures of the proposed pruning methods.

nodes.content: In the context of attempting to find small subnetworks that can be trained to the same accuracy as their dense parents, prior practice used IMP with reset-to-initialization ($k=0$). That procedure sometimes finds "winning tickets" for shallow networks but systematically fails for many deeper networks and larger tasks. The field therefore lacked a simple, general modification to IMP that would allow searching for subnetworks that reflect early, but nonzero, training progress. Such a modification is desirable because (i) small changes early in training may change the optimization dynamics of sparse subnetworks, (ii) a principled algorithmic rule is needed that does not rely on brittle per-architecture hyperparameter tuning (e.g., lowering learning rates or adding warmup bespoke to each network), and (iii) any practical early-pruning method must specify at which training iteration surviving weights should be fixed. The rewinding modification addresses this algorithmic gap by providing an explicit, reproducible variant of IMP that fixes surviving weights to their values at a chosen iteration $k$, enabling systematic exploration of pruning very early in training rather than strictly at iteration 0.

Prior to this work, demonstration of sparse subnetworks that train to match dense-network accuracy was largely limited to shallow models and small vision benchmarks. Attempts to apply the same reset-to-init IMP procedure to deeper networks and to large-scale tasks (ImageNet) either failed to find trainable subnetworks or required per-network hyperparameter changes (reduced learning rates or warmup), which undermines the claim that trainable subnetworks are present at initialization. Consequently, it was unclear whether sparse, trainable subnetworks exist in realistic deep networks early in training, and if so, how early and how sparse they can be. This absence of empirical evidence prevented claims that training cost could be reduced by pruning early in training at practically meaningful scales. The reported experiments directly address this gap by establishing concrete rewind iterations $k$ and corresponding sparsities for several deep ImageNet architectures, thereby expanding the set of known settings in which small subnetworks can complete training to match dense-model accuracy.

Before these definitions, explanations for when pruned subnetworks trained in isolation matched dense-network accuracy were qualitative and lacked a simple, measurable statistic capturing whether a subnetwork reaches the same optimization destination as the dense network or whether it does so consistently under SGD noise. The absence of such operational measures impeded mechanistic understanding of why some subnetworks (e.g., winning tickets) succeed whereas others fail and prevented a principled investigation into how early training dynamics affect trainability of pruned networks. By providing mathematically precise stability metrics tied to the training algorithm $\mathcal{A}^t$, researchers gain the ability to quantify the extent to which pruning perturbs final parameters and to relate such perturbations to final predictive performance.

The pre-contribution observation was that for deeper networks, the standard IMP procedure that resets surviving weights to their initial values often fails: the resulting subnetworks are not trainable to dense-model accuracy and are not measurably more stable than random masks. Practitioners responded with adhoc per-network changes (lower learning rates or warmup) that enable IMP-to-init to succeed in some cases, but these alterations are brittle and change the behavior of the unpruned dense network, complicating claims about the intrinsic presence of trainable subnetworks at initialization. What was missing was an experimentally-validated, architecture-agnostic alternative that preserves standard training hyperparameters while enabling recovery of trainable subnetworks. The empirical finding that modest rewinding or modest early warmup recovers trainable subnetworks closes this methodological gap and provides a less brittle path to early pruning for deep models.

Prior to this work, there was no quantitative demonstration that small amounts of early training progress systematically change the trainability of extreme sparse subnetworks in deep models, nor that an explicit stability metric would empirically track these changes. Without such a finding, it was unclear whether pruning should be attempted at iteration 0 or whether later early-training points might be more effective. By showing that stability improves rapidly in the earliest iterations and that these improvements mirror accuracy gains, the paper fills the explanatory gap linking early optimization dynamics to the emergence of trainable sparse subnetworks and motivates selecting an early rewinding point as a practical strategy for pruning.

The original lottery ticket statement posited that equally-capable sparse subnetworks could be found and reinitialized to their initial weights $W_0$. Empirical failures of reset-to-init IMP for many deep networks left ambiguity: either such subnetworks do not exist at initialization for some architectures, or existing search procedures fail to find them. A refined, more empirically-grounded hypothesis is needed that accounts for the observed empirical fact that subnetworks obtained by rewinding to an early iteration $k>0$ can consistently match dense-model accuracy. The revised hypothesis preserves the core scientific claim (existence of small trainable subnetworks) while relaxing the requirement that surviving weights be equal to the initial $W_0$, thereby aligning the hypothesis with the experimental reality for deeper networks and large tasks.

Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) can be modified to rewind surviving weights to their values at iteration $k$ (where $0 \ll k \ll T$) rather than resetting them to their initial values at iteration $0$. Concretely, execute IMP as follows: 1) initialize weights $W_0$ and mask $m=1^{|W_0|}$ (the trivial mask where all entries are 1); 2) train to iteration $k$ to obtain $W_k$; 3) continue training to $T$, prune lowest-magnitude remaining weights from $W_T$ to produce mask $m$; 4) reset surviving weights to $W_k$ (i.e., set surviving parameters to $m \odot W_k$) and repeat pruning iteratively if desired. This rewinding modification (IMP with $k \neq 0$) is an operational pruning procedure distinct from both resetting-to-init ($k=0$) and one-shot post-training pruning.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 is an algorithmic definition of the rewinding procedure. It is not an empirical claim; the derivation is a clear specification of the algorithm. No load-bearing weak points or distinguishing highlights apply beyond the clear documentation of the procedure.

nodes.title: Rewinding modification to Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP)

nodes.content: For multiple deep architectures and tasks, there exist fixed pruning masks $m$ and small rewind iterations $k$ (a few tenths of a percent to a few percent of total training) such that the subnetwork $m \odot W_k$, where $W_k$ are the network weights after $k$ training iterations, trains in the remaining training iterations to reach accuracy matching the original dense network (the network trained without pruning). Empirical instances include: ResNet-50 on ImageNet can be pruned to 70% sparsity (i.e., retaining 30% of weights) and match the original top-1 accuracy when rewound to epoch 4 (out of 90) and trained for the remaining epochs; Inception-v3 on ImageNet can be pruned to 70% sparsity and match original accuracy when rewound to epoch 6 (out of 171); SqueezeNet on ImageNet can be pruned to 50% sparsity and match original accuracy when rewound to epoch 10 (out of 150). For CIFAR-10 deeper models, rewinding to iteration 100 (VGG-19) or iteration 500 (ResNet-18) produces subnetworks found by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) that exceed the accuracy achievable when resetting to iteration 0. Across the networks studied, the rewinding points that enable matched accuracy lie in the range of approximately 0.1% to 7% of total training iterations, and achievable sparsities range from roughly 50% up to 70% sparsity on ImageNet examples and larger sparsities on smaller tasks.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 is supported by strong empirical evidence from multiple ImageNet architectures (H1), demonstrating existence of trainable subnetworks after early rewinding. No load-bearing weak points were identified within the stated scope of image classification. The consistency across architectures and use of standard hyperparameters gives high confidence in the existence claim.

nodes.title: Existence of trainable sparse subnetworks after a small number of training iterations for deep networks and ImageNet

nodes.content:
Let a subnetwork be the tuple $(W,m)$ where $W \in \mathbb{R}^D$ are weights and $m \in \{0,1\}^D$ is a fixed pruning mask; $m \odot W$ denotes elementwise masking. Let $\mathcal{A}^t: \mathbb{R}^D \times U \to \mathbb{R}^D$ be a stochastic training algorithm that maps initial weights and randomness $u \sim U$ (e.g., data-order randomness) to weights after $t$ iterations. For a distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ defined as the $L_2$ norm between masked parameters, the stability measures are defined as: (a) Stability to pruning of $(W_t,m)$ (where $W_t$ is the weights at iteration $t$ of training and $T$ is the total number of training iterations) is the expected distance
      $$
      d\big(\mathcal{A}^{\,T-t}(W_t, u),\; \mathcal{A}^{\,T-t}(m \odot W_t, u)\big)\quad\text{for }u\sim U,
      $$
      which measures how close a subnetwork trained in isolation arrives to the parameters the same subnetwork attains when trained as part of the full network; and (b) Stability to data order of $(W_t,m)$ is the expected distance
      $$
      d\big(\mathcal{A}^{\,T-t}(m \odot W_t, u),\; \mathcal{A}^{\,T-t}(m \odot W_t, u')\big)\quad\text{for }u,u'\sim U,
      $$
      which measures consistency of the subnetwork's final parameters under stochastic gradient descent (SGD) noise. These explicit definitions allow quantitative comparisons between subnetworks found by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) and randomly-pruned subnetworks using either $L_2$ distance or angle between masked parameter vectors.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 3 provides formal definitions with empirical validation (H2) showing the metrics discriminate between winning and losing tickets. No load-bearing weak points were identified; the definitions are precise and the validation is convincing.

nodes.title: Formal definitions of subnetwork stability (to pruning and to data order) and their measurement

nodes.content: Under standard learning-rate schedules and no special initialization treatment, iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) with resetting-to-iteration-0 fails to produce winning tickets (subnetworks that match the accuracy of the original dense network when trained from their retained weights) for many deeper networks (e.g., ResNet-18 and VGG-19 on CIFAR-10). Empirically, these IMP subnetworks at $k=0$ are no more stable (by the metrics of stability to pruning and stability to data order) nor more accurate than randomly-sampled subnetworks of the same size. Two remedies recover trainable subnetworks: (a) altering the learning schedule (reducing learning rate or adding warmup) enables IMP with $k=0$ to find winning tickets for some architectures, and (b) rewinding a small number of iterations into training (IMP with $k>0$) also recovers subnetworks that train to high accuracy without modifying the network's later training hyperparameters. Thus, failures of IMP at initialization can be remedied either by changing the early optimization dynamics (warmup or low learning rate) or by delaying the pruning decision by a small number of iterations and rewinding the surviving weights to their values at that earlier iteration.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4 is supported by controlled experiments (H4) that isolate rewinding iteration as the causal factor in recovery from IMP failure. The evidence covers multiple architectures and datasets. No load-bearing weak points compromise the claim within the tested configurations.

nodes.title: Empirical instability of Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) at iteration 0 for deeper networks and recovery via rewinding or early warmup

nodes.content: Measured stability (both stability to pruning and stability to data order) improves as the rewinding iteration $k$ increases from 0 into the early part of training, and these stability improvements closely track gains in final accuracy of the corresponding subnetworks. Empirically, for networks where iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) at $k=0$ (resetting to initialization) fails, the bulk of the improvement in stability and accuracy occurs within a small number of iterations: e.g., within the first ~100 iterations (≈0.14 epochs) for VGG-19 and within the first ~500 iterations (≈1.4 epochs) for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10; for ImageNet experiments, the subnetworks reach the accuracy of the original unpruned network (dense-model accuracy) after rewinding to epoch 4 (ResNet-50 / 90 total epochs), epoch 6 (Inception-v3 / 171 epochs), or epoch 10 (SqueezeNet / 150 epochs). Across many settings, subnetworks found by IMP that attain higher stability also attain higher accuracy than randomly-pruned subnetworks of the same size; the stability gap (the difference in stability between IMP-found and randomly-pruned subnetworks) explains a substantial portion of the accuracy gap (the difference in final accuracy between IMP-found and randomly-pruned subnetworks).

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 5 contains a correlational component (stability improvements track accuracy gains) which is strongly supported by broad evidence across architectures and datasets (H3). However, the additional claim that stability "explains a substantial portion of the accuracy gap" is threatened by P1: the evidence is only correlational, not causal, and the paper acknowledges the mechanism is unproven. Therefore, while the correlation is well-established, the explanatory interpretation carries significant uncertainty. The overall conclusion is credible for the correlational part but speculative for the causal part.

nodes.title: Stability improvements correlate with accuracy gains and accrue rapidly early in training

nodes.content: The lottery ticket hypothesis is revised to allow subnetworks that are fixed not at initialization but after a small amount of early training. Formally: consider a dense, randomly-initialized network $f(x;W_0)$ that when trained for $T^*$ iterations attains accuracy $a^*$. Let $W_t$ be the weights at iteration $t$ of training. There exist an iteration $k \ll T^*$ and a fixed pruning mask $m \in \{0,1\}^{|W_0|}$ with $||m||_1 \ll |W_0|$ (i.e., the number of retained weights is much smaller than total weights) such that the subnetwork $m \odot W_k$ trains to accuracy $a \ge a^*$ in at most $T \le T^* - k$ additional iterations. This statement generalizes the original winning-ticket formulation (which required rewinding to $W_0$) by permitting the retained weights to be rewound to their values at a small positive training iteration $k$ rather than to $W_0$.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 6 is a direct formal representation of the empirical pattern found in Conclusions 2 and 5. It is well-supported as an empirical hypothesis for image classification tasks. No independent weak points or highlights were identified; the confidence derives from the supporting conclusions. The hypothesis has not been tested beyond image classification, which is an acknowledged limitation.

nodes.title: Revised Lottery Ticket Hypothesis with Rewinding

nodes.content: In the empirical results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet image-classification tasks, the claim that the stability gap (the difference in $L_2$ distance between subnetworks found by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) and randomly-pruned subnetworks) "explains a substantial portion of the accuracy gap" is supported only by parallel trends showing that stability and accuracy improve together across rewinding iterations and across different networks. The study provides neither a causal mediation analysis nor an interventional manipulation (e.g., artificially changing stability while controlling for other factors) to separate the explanatory role of stability from confounding factors that improve simultaneously during early training, such as improved feature representations, reduced gradient noise magnitude, or better conditioning of the loss landscape.

metadata.failure_mode: If the stability gap does not causally explain the accuracy gap, then the specific component of Conclusion 5 that claims "the stability gap explains a substantial portion of the accuracy gap" is unsupported. The empirical evidence still supports correlation, but the stronger claim of explanation would be invalid. Consequently, the paper's mechanistic interpretation that stability provides a "window into the mechanism behind the lottery ticket hypothesis" becomes unjustified. The conclusion would narrow to a purely correlational observation, and the explanatory narrative connecting stability to trainability would not be supported.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's discussion explicitly states that the mechanism is not proven ("whether subnetworks that are more stable truly lie in the same optimization basin as the dense model is not proven"). The evidence for the "explains" claim is purely correlational. In the absence of causal identification, the assertion that stability directly causes accuracy improvements is speculative. This is a common pitfall in interpreting L2 parameter distances without theoretical justification tying distance to functional behavior.

nodes.title: Stability-gap explanation claim is correlational only

nodes.content: For ResNet-50 on ImageNet, rewinding to epoch 4 (out of 90 total epochs) with iterative magnitude pruning to 70% sparsity yields subnetworks that achieve a top-1 accuracy of 76.1 ± 0.1% (averaged over 5 trials), matching the dense network's accuracy of 76.1 ± 0.1%. This result is independently corroborated by similar matching on Inception-v3 (rewinding to epoch 6 out of 171, 70% sparsity, dense accuracy 78.1 ± 0.1%) and SqueezeNet (rewinding to epoch 10 out of 150, 50% sparsity, dense accuracy 54.8 ± 0.6%). All experiments use standard training hyperparameters for each architecture without per-architecture modification to the basic training schedule.

metadata.credit: Without these ImageNet-scale results, the claim that trainable sparse subnetworks exist for deep networks would remain limited to small-scale benchmarks (CIFAR-10). The consistency across three distinct ImageNet architectures (ResNet-50, Inception-v3, SqueezeNet) with different depths, parameter counts, and design patterns demonstrates that the rewinding strategy is not an artifact of a single architecture or hyperparameter tuning. This directly underwrites Conclusion 2 by providing concrete, reproducible existence proofs at practically meaningful sparsity levels (50-70%) on a large-scale task where prior pruning-at-initialization methods had failed. The fact that the subnetworks match dense accuracy within error bars further strengthens the claim.

nodes.title: ImageNet-scale empirical evidence for trainable subnetworks

nodes.content: On LeNet for MNIST and on ResNet-18 and VGG-19 for CIFAR-10 (with warmup or lower learning rate), the IMP-found winning tickets have data-order stability (L2 distance) values that are substantially lower than those of randomly-pruned subnetworks of the same size: e.g., LeNet at 10.7% sparsity shows data-order stability of 20.7 ± 0.6 for IMP vs. 58.6 ± 4.0 for random (2.8× improvement). The angle-based measurements show similar gaps. In contrast, for ResNet-18 (standard) and VGG-19 (standard) where IMP fails to find winning tickets, the IMP subnetworks have stability values indistinguishable from random (e.g., ResNet-18 standard: IMP 66.4 ± 0.7, random 66.7 ± 1.1).

metadata.credit: This validation establishes that the stability metrics are not abstract definitions but operationally discriminate between subnetworks that are trainable to high accuracy and those that are not. Without this evidence, the stability definitions would be arbitrary; the paper shows they capture a meaningful property of subnetworks. This supports Conclusion 3 by giving the definitions empirical grounding and supports Conclusion 5 by providing the metric that tracks accuracy.

nodes.title: Empirical validation of stability definitions

nodes.content: The correlation between stability (both data-order and pruning) and accuracy is demonstrated across six architectures: LeNet (MNIST), ResNet-18 (CIFAR-10, three hyperparameter variants), VGG-19 (CIFAR-10, three variants), ResNet-50 (ImageNet), Inception-v3 (ImageNet), and SqueezeNet (ImageNet). For each, the rewinding iteration is varied and both stability and accuracy are plotted. The trend is consistent: as rewinding iteration increases, stability improves (lower L2 distance) and accuracy rises in tandem. For networks where IMP at k=0 fails, the bulk of improvement in stability and accuracy occurs within small numbers of iterations (e.g., 100 iterations for VGG-19, 500 iterations for ResNet-18). Error bars (min/max for stability, standard deviation for accuracy) are reported.

metadata.credit: This breadth of evidence substantially reduces the risk that the stability-accuracy correlation is a spurious pattern specific to one setup. It covers small networks (LeNet) to large-scale networks (ResNet-50), small datasets (MNIST) to large datasets (ImageNet), and different training schedules. This directly underwrites the correlational component of Conclusion 5 by showing it holds across a diverse set of training regimes. Without this cross-scaling evidence, the claim that stability "closely tracks" accuracy could be dismissed as a narrow artifact.

nodes.title: Broad and consistent correlation evidence across architectures and datasets

nodes.content: For ResNet-18 and VGG-19 on CIFAR-10 under standard learning-rate schedules (momentum 0.1 with step decay at fixed epochs), rewinding IMP weights to iteration 0 produces no winning tickets (accuracy equal to random reinitialization). Changing only the rewinding iteration to 500 (ResNet-18) or 100 (VGG-19) while keeping all other training hyperparameters identical produces subnetworks that match or exceed the accuracy of the original dense network. This is contrasted with the alternative interventions studied in prior work (warmup, lower learning rate) which also recover winning tickets but change the dense training procedure itself.

metadata.credit: This controlled comparison isolates the rewinding iteration as the key variable: the same training hyperparameters that fail at iteration 0 succeed at iteration 100/500. Without this control, it would be unclear whether the success of rewinding is due to the extra training iterations, a different pruning mask, or some other factor. The direct comparison shows that the failure at initialization is not intrinsic to the architecture but is a property of the specific choice to reset to iteration 0. This directly supports Conclusion 4 by providing evidence that the failure can be remedied by a simple, hyperparameter-invariant change (delaying the pruning decision).

nodes.title: Controlled comparison isolating rewinding as causal factor

steps.reasoning: Define the notation used for weights and masks: let $W_0$ denote the vector of all network parameters at initialization, where $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^D$ and $D$ is the total number of parameters; let $m \in \{0,1\}^D$ denote a fixed pruning mask, and let $1^{|W_0|}$ denote the all-ones mask of the same dimensionality as $W_0$. Define the elementwise masking operation $m \odot W$ to set entries of $W$ to zero wherever $m$ has a zero and to retain entries where $m$ has a one.

Specify the training-iteration notation: let $W_t$ denote the weights after $t$ iterations of training (stochastic gradient descent or another optimizer) starting from $W_0$, and let $T$ denote the total number of iterations used for a full training run. Introduce the rewind index $k$ satisfying the paper's intended regime $0 \ll k \ll T$, meaning $k$ is a small positive integer much smaller than $T$.

Explain the rewind/reset operation precisely: after pruning produces a mask $m$ based on the weights $W_T$, the surviving parameters are set to their values at iteration $k$ by forming the vector $m \odot W_k$ (i.e., the surviving parameters are equal to $W_k$ on indices where $m=1$ and zero elsewhere). This distinguishes rewinding to $k$ from resetting to initialization ($k=0$), which would set surviving parameters to $m \odot W_0$.

State the operational distinction emphasized by the paper: treating $k$ as a hyperparameter yields a family of IMP procedures parameterized by $k$; the case $k=0$ recovers the original resetting-to-initialization variant of IMP, the case of pruning only once after training corresponds to choosing $k=T$ (i.e., pruning as a one-shot post-training operation), and choosing $0<k<T$ defines an intermediate operational procedure that is evaluated throughout the work as "IMP with rewinding" or "IMP with $k\neq 0$."

Note the paper's characterization of the rewinding modification as the primary algorithmic change evaluated: this modified IMP (IMP with $k\neq 0$) is presented and evaluated throughout the experiments, and the authors explicitly describe it as an operational pruning procedure that is distinct from both resetting-to-init ($k=0$) and one-shot post-training pruning.

Treat the following upstream results as established and available for use: (a) the IMP-with-rewinding procedure and its operational definition are known (conclusion 1), and (b) the empirical relationship between early rewinding, improved subnetwork stability, and improved subnetwork accuracy is known (conclusion 5). Symbols used below: $k$ denotes rewind iteration or epoch, $T$ denotes total training iterations or epochs, $m \odot W_k$ denotes the rewound masked subnetwork, and "sparsity" denotes the fraction of parameters set to zero by the mask $m$.

Present the ImageNet experimental evidence that small-$k$ rewinding yields trainable sparse subnetworks of deep architectures: the paper reports experiments on ResNet-50, Inception-v3, and SqueezeNet trained on ImageNet with standard training schedules where rewinding to small positive epochs yields subnetworks that, when trained for the remaining budget, match the original network's top-1 accuracy at substantial sparsities. Specifically, the ImageNet experiments table reports that ResNet-50 can be pruned to $70\%$ sparsity (retaining $30\%$ of weights) and match the original top-1 accuracy when rewound to epoch $4$ out of $90$ total epochs; Inception-v3 can be pruned to $70\%$ sparsity and match original accuracy when rewound to epoch $6$ out of $171$; SqueezeNet can be pruned to $50\%$ sparsity and match original accuracy when rewound to epoch $10$ out of $150$.

Present supporting CIFAR-10 evidence that rewinding to early iterations produces subnetworks that exceed resetting-to-initialization performance: for CIFAR-10 deeper models, the paper reports that rewinding to iteration $100$ for VGG-19 and iteration $500$ for ResNet-18 produces IMP subnetworks that attain higher accuracy than the same IMP procedure with resetting-to-iteration-$0$, consistent with the observed rapid accrual of stability and accuracy with small positive $k$ in those networks.

Summarize the ranges of rewinding percentages and achievable sparsities reported: across the networks studied, the rewinding points that enable matched dense accuracy lie in the range of approximately $0.1\%$ to $7\%$ of total training iterations/epochs (examples above are $4/90 \approx 4.4\%$, $6/171 \approx 3.5\%$, $10/150 \approx 6.6\%$), and the authors report achievable sparsities from roughly $50\%$ up to extreme values such as $70\%$ sparsity in ImageNet experiments and still larger sparsities on smaller tasks.

Synthesize the conclusion: therefore, for multiple deep architectures and tasks, there exist fixed pruning masks $m$ and small rewind iterations $k$ (a few tenths of a percent to a few percent of total training) such that the subnetwork $m \odot W_k$ trains in the remaining budget to reach accuracy matching the original dense network; empirical instances include ResNet-50 on ImageNet pruned to $70\%$ and matched when rewound to epoch $4$ (of $90$), Inception-v3 on ImageNet pruned to $70\%$ and matched when rewound to epoch $6$ (of $171$), SqueezeNet on ImageNet pruned to $50\%$ and matched when rewound to epoch $10$ (of $150$), and CIFAR-10 deeper models with rewinding to iteration $100$ (VGG-19) or $500$ (ResNet-18) outperforming resetting-to-$0$.

Define a subnetwork and masking notation used throughout: a subnetwork is the tuple $(W,m)$ where $W \in \mathbb{R}^D$ denotes weights and $m \in \{0,1\}^D$ denotes a fixed pruning mask; $m \odot W$ denotes the elementwise product of $m$ and $W$, producing the masked parameter vector that zeroes pruned entries.

Define the stochastic training algorithm and noise model used in the stability definitions: let $\mathcal{A}^t: \mathbb{R}^D \times U \to \mathbb{R}^D$ denote the (possibly randomized) training algorithm run for $t$ iterations, where $\mathcal{A}^t(W, u)$ returns the parameter vector after $t$ iterations when starting from parameters $W$ and using randomness $u$, and where $u$ is drawn from a distribution $U$ that captures sources of stochasticity such as data-order randomness in minibatch sampling.

Define the distance metric used in the paper: for two parameter vectors $W$ and $W'$, and a mask $m$, define the distance $d(W,W')$ to be the $L_2$ norm between the masked parameter vectors, i.e., $d(W,W') = \| m \odot W - m \odot W' \|_2$. State that the paper also performs parallel analyses using the angle between masked parameter vectors as an alternative measure (reported in appendices and angle figures).
Fig. 10

Define stability to pruning formally: for a subnetwork $(W_t,m)$ with $W_t$ denoting weights at iteration $t$, the stability to pruning (with respect to randomness $u\sim U$ and distance $d$) is the expected value over $u$ of the distance
$$
d\big(\mathcal{A}^{\,T-t}(W_t, u),\; \mathcal{A}^{\,T-t}(m \odot W_t, u)\big),
$$
which measures how close the final masked parameters are when the subnetwork is trained in isolation versus when the same subnetwork's weights are those arising inside the full network.

Define stability to data order formally: for the same subnetwork $(W_t,m)$, the stability to data order (with respect to $u,u' \sim U$ and distance $d$) is the expected value over independent draws $u,u'$ of the distance
$$
d\big(\mathcal{A}^{\,T-t}(m \odot W_t, u),\; \mathcal{A}^{\,T-t}(m \odot W_t, u')\big),
$$
which measures the consistency of the subnetwork's final masked parameters under different stochastic realizations of the training process (e.g., different minibatch orders).

State how these definitions are used operationally in the experiments: the paper computes these expected distances empirically by training multiple instances (with different data-order randomness $u$) of the full network and of the masked subnetwork, measuring $L_2$ distances and also measuring angles between resulting masked parameter vectors; these measures permit quantitative comparisons between subnetworks found by IMP and randomly-pruned subnetworks of the same size.
Fig. 3

State the meaning of "IMP with resetting-to-iteration-0": set $k=0$ in the IMP procedure, so surviving weights after pruning are reset to $m \odot W_0$ where $W_0$ denotes the initialization; this is the variant studied by Frankle and Carbin and referred to as the original IMP/winning-ticket procedure.

Present empirical evidence that IMP at $k=0$ fails on deeper networks (VGG-19 and Resnet-18) under standard learning-rate schedules: the paper displays loss/accuracy and winning-ticket behavior showing that, for these architectures trained on CIFAR-10 with standard schedules, IMP at $k=0$ does not produce winning tickets (i.e., pruned-and-reinitialized subnetworks do not match original dense-network accuracy). This observation is summarized in the discussion of Figure 1 and in the accompanying Table of network configurations and "Winning?" columns.
Fig. 1
Fig. 2

Present the empirical observation that IMP subnetworks at $k=0$ are not more stable nor more accurate than randomly-sampled subnetworks for these failing cases: the paper reports measurements of both data-order stability and pruning stability (distance and angle) in Figure 3 and accompanying tables showing that for Resnet-18 (standard) and VGG-19 (standard) the distances/angles and accuracies of IMP subnetworks reset to iteration 0 are comparable to those of randomly-pruned subnetworks of the same sparsity, indicating no stability or accuracy advantage at initialization.
Fig. 3

Describe the first remedy: altering early optimization dynamics. The paper reports that reducing the learning rate (a "low" learning-rate configuration) or adding a learning-rate warmup period changes early training dynamics and enables IMP with $k=0$ to find winning tickets on some architectures (evidence given in the table of networks and "Winning?" outcomes and in the improved stability and accuracy numbers for the 'low' and 'warmup' variants of Resnet-18 and VGG-19). These altered schedules yield IMP subnetworks that are both more stable and more accurate than random subnetworks under the same conditions.
Fig. 2

Describe the second remedy: rewinding a small number of iterations. The paper modifies IMP to rewind to a small positive iteration $k>0$ (IMP with $k\neq 0$ as established in the algorithm) and then empirically shows that rewinding recovers subnetworks that train to high accuracy without changing the network's later training hyperparameters. Specifically, in the cases where IMP at $k=0$ fails, rewinding a small number of iterations produces subnetworks that become substantially more stable (by both pruning- and data-order stability measures) and attain much higher accuracy. These results are reported in the rewinding experiments and stability-versus-rewind plots.
Fig. 4

Synthesize the empirical conclusion: therefore, failures of IMP at initialization can be remedied either by modifying the early optimization dynamics (lower learning rate or warmup) or by delaying the pruning decision by a small number of iterations and rewinding to those weights (IMP with $k>0$). This is supported by the comparative stability and accuracy numbers across the standard, low, and warmup learning schedules as well as the rewinding experiments.

Treat the following upstream results as established and available for use: (a) the rewinding variant of IMP (IMP with $k\neq 0$) and its operational definition are known (conclusion 1), and (b) the formal definitions and empirical measurement procedures for subnetwork stability (stability to pruning and stability to data order, measured via $L_2$ distance or angle between masked parameter vectors) are known (conclusion 3). Symbols used below: $k$ denotes the rewinding iteration, $T$ denotes total training iterations, $m \odot W_k$ denotes the rewound masked subnetwork, and $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the $L_2$ distance between masked parameter vectors.

State the empirical observation relating stability to rewinding iteration: across the networks studied, as the rewinding iteration $k$ increases from $0$ into the early part of training, both measures of stability (stability to pruning and stability to data order) improve monotonically or rapidly in the initial phase. This trend is shown in the experiments that plot stability versus rewinding iteration and is reproduced across architectures (CIFAR-10 networks and ImageNet networks).
Fig. 4

State the empirical observation relating accuracy to rewinding iteration: the paper shows that the final accuracy attained by subnetworks rewound to iteration $k$ also increases as $k$ increases from $0$ into the early portion of training, and that the improvements in accuracy closely track the improvements in stability as a function of $k$ in the plotted experimental curves (stability-versus-k and accuracy-versus-k plots).
Fig. 4

Provide concrete, reported quantitative timings for the rapid accrual of stability and accuracy in CIFAR-10 deeper models: for VGG-19 on CIFAR-10, the bulk of stability and accuracy improvement occurs within the first approximately $100$ iterations (which the paper reports as approximately $0.14$ epochs under that training schedule); for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, the bulk of the improvement occurs within approximately $500$ iterations (reported as about $1.4$ epochs). These numerical values are reported in the text summarizing the stability-versus-rewind results.
Fig. 4

Provide concrete, reported quantitative rewinding epochs for ImageNet experiments where subnetworks attain dense-model accuracy: for ResNet-50 trained for $90$ epochs total, rewinding to epoch $4$ yields a 70%-sparse subnetwork that matches the original top-1 accuracy; for Inception-v3 trained for $171$ epochs, rewinding to epoch $6$ yields a 70%-sparse subnetwork that matches original accuracy; for SqueezeNet trained for $150$ epochs, rewinding to epoch $10$ yields a 50%-sparse subnetwork that matches original accuracy. These values are reported in the ImageNet experimental section and summarized in the ImageNet results table.
Fig. 6
Fig. 7

State the comparative observation that subnetworks found by IMP that attain higher measured stability also attain higher final accuracy than randomly-pruned subnetworks of the same size: the experiments show that as the stability gap between IMP subnetworks and randomly-pruned subnetworks grows with increasing $k$, the corresponding accuracy gap also grows, and the authors argue that the stability gap explains a substantial portion of the accuracy gap (this claim is made in the discussion and supported by the parallel trends observed in the plotted curves).
Fig. 4

Synthesize the conclusion: therefore, measured stability improvements (both to pruning and to data order) accrue rapidly in the early iterations of training as $k$ increases from $0$, and these stability improvements closely track and correlate with gains in final accuracy of the corresponding subnetworks; for networks where IMP at $k=0$ fails, the bulk of stability and accuracy improvements occur within a small number of iterations early in training (e.g., $\sim$100 iterations for VGG-19, $\sim$500 for ResNet-18), and for ImageNet examples the rewinding epochs that enable matched dense accuracy are at small percentages of total training (examples: epoch 4 of 90 for ResNet-50, epoch 6 of 171 for Inception-v3, epoch 10 of 150 for SqueezeNet).

Treat the following upstream results as established and available for use: (a) the empirical existence of trainable sparse subnetworks after small amounts of training for deep networks and ImageNet (conclusion 2), and (b) the empirical relationship that small positive rewinding iterations $k$ rapidly improve subnetwork stability and accuracy (conclusion 5). Symbols used below: $f(x;W_0)$ denotes a dense, randomly-initialized network with initial parameters $W_0$, $T^*$ denotes the total iterations the dense network is trained for, and $a^*$ denotes the accuracy attained by the dense network after $T^*$ iterations.

Reproduce the formal revised statement of the lottery ticket hypothesis with rewinding as presented in the paper: consider a dense, randomly-initialized network $f(x;W_0)$ that when trained for $T^*$ iterations attains accuracy $a^*$. There exist an iteration $k \ll T^*$ and a fixed pruning mask $m \in \{0,1\}^{|W_0|}$ with $\|m\|_1 \ll |W_0|$ such that the subnetwork $m \odot W_k$ trains to accuracy $a \ge a^*$ in at most $T \le T^* - k$ additional iterations. (This is the paper's formal statement of the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis with Rewinding and directly generalizes the original winning-ticket formulation by allowing rewinding to $W_k$ for a small positive $k$.)

Explain the empirical motivation connecting the revised formal statement to the experiments: the ImageNet and CIFAR-10 experiments demonstrate concrete instances of masks $m$ and small rewinding iterations $k$ such that $m \odot W_k$ trains within the remaining budget to match or exceed dense-network accuracy, supporting the existence clause in the revised hypothesis; the stability measurements provide a mechanisms-based rationale for why rewinding to $W_k$ permits the subnetwork to reach the same destination as the dense network and so attain comparable accuracy.
Fig. 7

Conclude that the revised hypothesis generalizes the original by permitting the retained weights to be rewound to their values at a small positive training iteration $k$ rather than requiring $k=0$ (initialization), and note the paper's explicit formalization of this generalization both in the introduction and in the concluding summarization of the "Lottery Ticket Hypothesis with Rewinding."

open_questions.content: The paper explicitly acknowledges and leaves unresolved several scientific and practical issues: (1) Efficient discovery: the presented rewinding-IMP procedure requires training the dense network one or more times to locate a mask and rewind point; the development of efficient methods that locate equally-capable subnetworks at an early iteration $k$ without repeated full training remains open. (2) Existence at initialization: it remains unresolved whether, for some architectures and sparsity regimes, equally-capable subnetworks truly exist at iteration 0 and are merely undetected by IMP, or whether their absence is intrinsic; determining which of these is the case requires either improved search methods or theoretical characterization. (3) Scope beyond image classification: experiments are limited to image-classification benchmarks (CIFAR-10 and ImageNet); it is an open question whether analogous rewinding-era subnetworks and stability phenomena hold in other domains (e.g., NLP, reinforcement learning, generative models). (4) Practical performance gains and structured pruning: the work uses unstructured magnitude pruning, which does not directly yield execution speedups on commodity hardware; extending these findings to structured pruning techniques or developing hardware-aware sparse training methods that exploit early pruning remains unresolved. (5) Mechanistic theory: while stability metrics correlate with accuracy, a theoretical explanation of why small amounts of early training produce so large a change in subnetwork trainability (e.g., basin-of-attraction dynamics, role of optimization noise) is not established; in particular, whether subnetworks that are more stable truly lie in the same optimization basin as the dense model is not proven. (6) Extending the rewinding range and automating $k$ selection: determining principled criteria to select the rewind iteration $k$ automatically (and whether that $k$ generalizes across seeds/architectures) is left for future work. These open issues and limitations are explicitly discussed in the paper and mark directions for follow-up research.
